text: 1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background and motivation

Telecommunications companies sell services on recurring plans, so the value of a customer builds up month after month, and a departure removes all the revenue that would have followed. Two practical questions follow. First, *how much revenue does a customer generate over their life with the company?* Second, *which customers are likely to leave?* Both are prediction problems. The first asks for a number and is solved with regression; the second asks for a yes/no answer and is solved with classification. Together they let a company focus its retention effort on customers who are both at risk and valuable.

This project uses the IBM Telco Customer Churn data set (7,043 customers, 20 attributes) to study both problems with the methods of a first course in predictive analytics: data preprocessing, correlation analysis, simple, multiple and polynomial regression, logistic regression, k-nearest neighbours, Naive Bayes, decision trees, Random Forest and support vector machines, evaluated with MAE, MSE, RMSE, R-squared, accuracy, log loss, AUC, precision, recall, F1 score and the confusion matrix.
1.2 Problem statement

**Part A (regression).** Predict the lifetime revenue of a customer, measured by *TotalCharges* (USD billed to date), from the customer's account and service attributes, using four regression models, and select the best model for prediction. **Part B (classification).** Predict whether a customer will churn (*Churn* = Yes; 1,869 of 7,043 customers, 26.5%), using six classifiers, and select the best classifier. Finally, combine the two selected models to rank customers by risk and revenue.
1.3 Objectives
Seven specific, measurable and non-overlapping objectives were fixed before modelling. Each is answered with actual results in Chapter 4.

2. SOURCE OF DATASET
2.1 Provenance

The data set is the *Telco Customer Churn* sample data published by IBM as part of its Cognos Analytics sample data sets. It describes a **fictional** telecommunications company that provides home phone and internet services. IBM generated it as a teaching and benchmarking resource, so it is realistic in structure but is not a record of the customers of a real operator. Findings describe patterns in a benchmark data set and should not be presented as facts about any real company.

2.2 Description of the data

Each row is one customer. The columns fall into four groups: the churn label; the services subscribed to (phone, multiple lines, internet type, online security, online backup, device protection, technical support, streaming TV and streaming movies); account information (tenure, contract, payment method, paperless billing, monthly and total charges); and demographics (gender, senior-citizen flag, partner and dependents).

text: 2.3 Why this dataset was chosen

items: **Two natural prediction targets.** TotalCharges is a continuous number (regression) and Churn is a binary label (classification), so one data set serves Units II and III of the syllabus.
**Right size.** 7,043 rows are enough for stable train, validation and test sets and small enough to run every analysis within minutes.
**Mixed variable types.** Numeric, binary and multi-level categorical columns call for encoding and scaling (Unit I).
**Interpretable domain.** Contract, tenure and charges have direct business meaning, so results are easy to explain.

text: 2.4 Limitations of the dataset

items: The company is fictional and the data are a single snapshot; there are no dates, so true temporal validation is impossible.
*Churn* means leaving within the last month, so the rate is a point-in-time proportion, not a rate per period.
There is no usage, network-quality, complaint or competitor information, which real churn models rely on.

TotalCharges is billing history up to the snapshot. It is almost arithmetic in tenure and monthly charge (Section 4.3), so predicting it is a good exercise in regression but is not a forecast of *future* revenue.

3.3 Preprocessing: encoding and scaling

Machine-learning models need numbers. The 15 categorical attributes are converted to 0/1 indicator columns (one-hot encoding), and numeric inputs are standardised (z = (x - mean) / standard deviation) for the models that depend on distances or gradients (linear models, kNN, Naive Bayes, SVM). Tree-based models do not need scaling. After encoding, the inputs of the classification models have 45 columns. Both steps are placed inside scikit-learn Pipelines, so the means, standard deviations and categories are learned from training data only.
3.4 Target variables

In Part B the target is imbalanced: 5,174 customers stayed (73.5%) and 1,869 churned (26.5%). A model that always predicts "stay" would reach 73.5% accuracy and find no churner, so accuracy alone is not enough; precision, recall, F1 and AUC are reported as well, and a majority-class baseline shows what "no skill" looks like. In Part A the target is TotalCharges, a right-skewed number from 0 to about 8,700 USD.

text: 4. ANALYSIS ON DATASET

This chapter reports seven analyses. Each follows the prescribed structure: (i) Introduction, (ii) General Description, (iii) Specific Requirements, Functions and Formulas, (iv) Analysis Results, and (v) Visualization with interpretation. Every number in the tables and text is produced by the notebook and stored in the results folder.
4.1 Objective O1: Understanding the data
i. Introduction

Before any model is built, an analyst needs to know how the variables relate to each other and which customer groups churn most. Correlation shows which numeric variables move together; comparing churn rates across groups shows where the problem is concentrated and which attributes are unlikely to help a model.
ii. General Description

Three things are examined: the Pearson correlation between the numeric variables and the two targets; the average of each numeric variable for churners and stayers; and the churn rate in every group of every categorical attribute. For each attribute the *spread* (highest group rate minus lowest group rate) summarises how much the attribute separates churners from stayers.
iii. Specific Requirements, Functions and Formulas

text: The Pearson correlation coefficient between two variables x and y with n observations is:
r = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / √( Σ (xᵢ − x̄)² · Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)² )        (1)

r lies between −1 (perfect negative linear relationship) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 means no linear relationship. With the binary churn indicator (0/1), r measures how strongly a numeric variable differs between churners and stayers. The spread of an attribute is:
spread = max over groups of churn rate − min over groups of churn rate        (2)

4.2 Objective O2: Simple Linear Regression
i. Introduction

The simplest way to predict a number is a straight line through one input. For lifetime revenue, the natural input is tenure: the longer a customer stays, the more they have been billed. This objective measures how far a straight line in tenure alone can go.
ii. General Description

TotalCharges is the target (y) and tenure in months is the single input (x). The line is fitted on the training set by Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), which chooses the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals. The slope and intercept are calculated by hand from the closed-form formulas and checked against scikit-learn. The fit is judged on the training and test sets with MAE, MSE, RMSE and R-squared, and the residuals are inspected for patterns.
iii. Specific Requirements, Functions and Formulas

caption: Functions used in O2
head: Purpose
Function

text: The model is ŷ = β₀ + β₁x. OLS minimises the sum of squared errors, giving:
β₁ = Σ (xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ (xᵢ − x̄)²,     β₀ = ȳ − β₁x̄        (3)
For several inputs the same idea is written in matrix form (the normal equation), which is used again in O3:
β = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy        (4)
The evaluation metrics, with n test observations, actual values yᵢ, predictions ŷᵢ and mean ȳ, are:
MAE = (1/n) Σ |yᵢ − ŷᵢ|,     MSE = (1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²,     RMSE = √MSE        (5)
R² = 1 − Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² / Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)²        (6)

MAE is the average size of the error in dollars; MSE squares the errors and so punishes large ones; RMSE brings MSE back to dollars; R² is the share of the variation in y that the model explains (1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean).

At each tenure the points fan out into a band: customers with a low monthly bill sit near the bottom of the fan and customers with a high bill near the top, and the single line runs through the middle. 4.3 Objective O3: Multiple and Polynomial Regression
i. Introduction

O2 showed that tenure alone leaves a fan-shaped error. Two natural improvements are to use more inputs (Multiple Linear Regression) and to let the model bend and combine inputs (Polynomial Regression). This objective tests how much each helps.
ii. General Description

Multiple Linear Regression uses SeniorCitizen, tenure, MonthlyCharges and the 15 one-hot encoded categorical attributes, 18 inputs in the sense of columns before encoding. Polynomial Regression takes tenure and MonthlyCharges, standardises them, creates powers and products up to a chosen degree, and fits a linear model on those new columns. The degree (1 to 5) is chosen on the validation set as the one with the lowest RMSE; a higher degree always fits the fit set at least as well, so the validation set is what reveals overfitting.
iii. Specific Requirements, Functions and Formulas

In Equation 8, the product term tm lets the effect of tenure depend on the monthly charge. This matches how billing works: total charges are roughly the monthly charge multiplied by the number of months.

text: Multiple Linear Regression, fitted with all inputs, has a test R² of 0.900 and a test RMSE of USD 702, compared with 0.657 and USD 1,297 for tenure alone. Adding inputs helps a great deal, but the model is still linear and cannot represent the tenure-by-charge product. The coefficients of the categorical inputs in the table are mostly small adjustments that compensate for the missing interaction, not business effects, and should not be read as causes.

**Why the polynomial model is so accurate.** For customers with tenure above zero, TotalCharges divided by (tenure x MonthlyCharges) has a median of 1.00, and 80% of customers lie within 5% of exactly 1. TotalCharges is therefore close to the product of tenure and monthly charge by the way bills accumulate. A degree-2 polynomial contains that product, so it fits almost perfectly. This is a legitimate regression result, but the very high R² reflects a near-arithmetical relationship in the data and should not be presented as a deep discovery.

**Conclusion of O3.** More inputs reduce the error a lot, and allowing the tenure-by-charge product reduces it by another order of magnitude. Degree 2 is enough.
4.4 Objective O4: Comparing four regression models
i. Introduction

With three regression ideas in hand, the practical question is which model should be used for prediction. A fair comparison needs the same data for every model, a selection rule fixed in advance, and a look at both training and test error to detect overfitting.
ii. General Description

Four models are compared: (1) Simple Linear Regression on tenure, (2) Multiple Linear Regression on all inputs, (3) Polynomial Regression of the degree chosen in O3, and (4) Random Forest Regression on all inputs. The Random Forest settings (maximum depth and minimum leaf size) are chosen from a 12-combination grid on the validation set. **Selection rule, fixed before the test set was used:** the model with the lowest validation RMSE wins, and if models are within 1% of each other the simpler one is preferred. The winner is refitted on the full training set and its test scores are reported with MAE, MSE, RMSE and R².

4.5 Objective O5: Comparing six classifiers for churn
i. Introduction

Part B asks a yes/no question: will this customer churn? Many algorithms can answer it, and none is best everywhere. The syllabus covers six that differ in how they learn, and this objective compares them on equal terms.
ii. General Description

The six classifiers are Logistic Regression, k-Nearest Neighbours, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest and Support Vector Machine, together with a majority-class baseline that always predicts "stay". All use the same encoded inputs and the same train, validation and test sets. One setting of each model is tuned on the validation set by the **F1 score**, because churners are a minority and F1 balances precision and recall. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest and SVM use balanced class weights, which make errors on churners count more. The final scores use the default threshold of 0.5.
iii. Specific Requirements, Functions and Formulas

caption: Functions used in O5
head: Model
scikit-learn class
Setting tuned

text: Algorithms in brief

**Logistic Regression** turns a weighted sum of the inputs into a probability with the logistic (sigmoid) function (Hosmer, Lemeshow and Sturdivant, 2013). **k-Nearest Neighbours** is a *lazy* learner: it stores the training data and predicts the majority class among the k closest customers (Cover and Hart, 1967). **Naive Bayes** applies Bayes' theorem and assumes the inputs are independent given the class (Domingos and Pazzani, 1997). **A Decision Tree** asks a sequence of yes/no questions on the inputs, choosing each split to make the groups purer, which gives readable rules (Breiman et al., 1984). **A Random Forest** averages many trees (Breiman, 2001). **A Support Vector Machine** finds the boundary with the widest margin between the classes, and the RBF kernel lets that boundary curve (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995).
P(churn | x) = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + β_p x_p))        (10)
P(C | x) ∝ P(C) · Π_j P(x_j | C),     d(a, b) = √( Σ_j (a_j − b_j)² ),     Gini = 1 − Σ_k p_k²        (11)

Equation 11 shows the Naive Bayes rule, the Euclidean distance used by kNN and the Gini impurity used by decision trees. The evaluation measures are, with TP, FP, TN and FN the counts of the confusion matrix:
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / n,     Precision = TP / (TP + FP),     Recall = TP / (TP + FN)        (12)
F1 = 2 · Precision · Recall / (Precision + Recall),     LogLoss = −(1/n) Σ [ yᵢ ln pᵢ + (1 − yᵢ) ln(1 − pᵢ) ]        (13)

AUC is the area under the ROC curve, which plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the threshold moves; it equals the probability that a randomly chosen churner gets a higher score than a randomly chosen stayer (Fawcett, 2006). 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect. Log loss measures how good the predicted *probabilities* are, and punishes confident wrong answers heavily; lower is better.

text: Every real model is far better than the baseline: the baseline reaches 73.5% accuracy but its recall and F1 are zero because it never predicts churn. Among the six classifiers, the differences are modest. Logistic Regression and Random Forest tie for the best AUC (0.841); k-Nearest Neighbours has the best accuracy (0.779) and best log loss but the lowest recall of the six (0.575); Naive Bayes has the highest recall (0.837) but the lowest accuracy (0.695) and a very high log loss (2.75).

The log-loss values need care. Naive Bayes produces overconfident probabilities because the independence assumption counts related inputs (for example the several services) several times, so when it is wrong it is wrong with near-certainty. Class weights also push probabilities of the balanced models upwards, which raises their log loss relative to kNN. The F1 scores of the six models lie between 0.580 and 0.634; with only 374 churners in the test set, differences of about 0.01 are within noise.

**Conclusion of O5.** All six classifiers are far better than the baseline and close to each other; the choice depends on whether accuracy or recall matters more, which is why the selection rule below is stated explicitly.
4.6 Objective O6: Selecting the best classifier; rules and errors
i. Introduction

Choosing a model is only half of the job. A manager also wants to know *why* it predicts churn, and an analyst wants to know where it fails. A shallow decision tree gives readable rules, the Random Forest gives an importance score for every input, and an error profile shows which churners are missed.
ii. General Description

**Selection rule, fixed before the test set was used:** the classifier with the highest validation F1 is chosen. This favours models that find churners without flooding the retention team with false alarms. Then three things are produced: the rules of a depth-3 decision tree; the importance of the inputs in the Random Forest; and an error profile of the selected classifier on the test set (true and false positives and negatives, and the share of churners missed in several groups).

text: Importance(j) = Σ over splits on input j of (impurity decrease × share of samples reaching the split), averaged over all trees        (14)

Equation 14 describes the importance used by the Random Forest: an input that is often used for splits near the top of many trees, and that makes the groups much purer, gets a high score. The scores sum to 1. They show which inputs the model uses, not whether the relationship is causal.

text: **Random Forest** has the highest validation F1 (0.6322) and is selected, although the margin over Logistic Regression (0.6258) and SVM (0.6251) is small. On the test set it achieves accuracy 0.769, AUC 0.841, precision 0.548, recall 0.754, F1 0.634 and log loss 0.462: it identifies 282 of 374 churners and raises 233 false alarms.

**Decision-tree rules.** A tree limited to depth 3 can be read as a short list of rules (Figure 14). Customers on a month-to-month contract with fibre-optic internet are classified as churners; month-to-month customers without fibre are classified as churners only if their tenure is at most 5 months; customers on longer contracts are classified as stayers. This tiny tree reaches test accuracy 0.746, recall 0.783 and F1 0.621, close to the full forest, which shows that most of the useful signal is in a few simple rules.

4.7 Objective O7: Using both selected models together
i. Introduction

The two parts of the project answer different questions. The regression model says how much revenue a customer has generated, and the classifier says how likely the customer is to leave. A company would like to know which customers are *both* valuable and at risk. This objective combines the two predictions.
ii. General Description

For every customer in the test set, the selected regression model (Polynomial Regression) gives a predicted TotalCharges and the selected classifier (Random Forest) gives a churn probability. Customers are placed in four groups using two cut-offs: a churn probability of 0.5 and the median predicted TotalCharges (USD 1,380). The actual churn rate in each group is then checked against what really happened.

text: The grouping is informative. Customers flagged as high risk actually churn at 61% (lower-revenue group) and 42% (high-revenue group), while those flagged as low risk churn at only about 11% and 10%. The **165 customers who are both high risk and high revenue** (mean predicted TotalCharges USD 2,998, mean monthly bill USD 90) are the natural first target for a retention offer.

One caution applies. TotalCharges is revenue *to date*, so a low value often just means a new customer. The "lower revenue" high-risk group (mostly recent month-to-month customers) may still be valuable in the future; the grouping ranks past revenue, not future value.

5. CONCLUSION
The project analysed the IBM Telco Customer Churn data with the methods of the syllabus and answered each of the seven objectives with evidence.

items: **O1 (data).** The data are clean apart from 11 blank TotalCharges (tenure zero). Tenure, contract, internet service and protection services separate churners from stayers; gender and phone service do not. TotalCharges is strongly correlated with tenure (r = 0.83) and monthly charge (r = 0.65).
**O2 (Simple Linear Regression).** TotalCharges = -201.0 + 77.0 x tenure. Test R² = 0.657, RMSE USD 1,297; the residuals fan out with tenure.
**O3 (Multiple and Polynomial).** More inputs lift test R² to 0.900; a degree-2 polynomial in tenure and monthly charge reaches 0.999, because total charges are close to tenure times monthly charge.
**O4 (regression comparison).** Polynomial Regression is selected: validation RMSE USD 65.1, test RMSE USD 66.2, MAE USD 44.9, no overfitting. Random Forest is a close second.
**O5 (classification comparison).** All six classifiers beat the baseline with similar AUC (0.80 to 0.84) and F1 (0.58 to 0.63); they differ mainly in how they trade accuracy against recall.

**O6 (best classifier).** Random Forest is selected by validation F1 (test accuracy 0.769, AUC 0.841, recall 0.754, F1 0.634). Its behaviour reduces to rules on contract, internet service and tenure; it misses churn among long-tenure, contracted customers.

**O7 (combined use).** The two selected models rank customers into four groups with actual churn rates from about 10% to 61% and identify 165 high-risk, high-revenue customers as the first retention target.

text: 5.1 Recommendations

items: Use the polynomial regression model to estimate customer lifetime revenue to date, and the Random Forest to flag customers at risk of churning.
Focus retention effort first on customers who are high risk and high revenue, then on new month-to-month customers, where churn is highest.
Encourage month-to-month customers to move to annual contracts, and examine why fibre-optic and electronic-check customers churn more.
Offer online security and technical support to customers who lack them, and test the effect before scaling it.
Treat long-tenure and annual-contract customers separately, because the classifier misses most of their churn.

text: 5.2 Limitations

items: The company is fictional and the data are a single snapshot; results show a method and should not be generalised to a real operator.
Relationships are associations, not causes.
TotalCharges is almost arithmetic in tenure and monthly charge, so the near-perfect regression fit is expected; it is not a forecast of future revenue.
A single train/validation/test split was used. With 374 churners in the test set, small differences between classifiers are not meaningful.
Classifier settings were tuned over small grids, and the best k for kNN lay at the edge of its grid.
No temporal validation was possible because the data carry no dates.

text: 6. FUTURE SCOPE

items: **Forward-looking revenue.** Predict TotalCharges from information known at sign-up (excluding tenure) or predict revenue over the next months, to make the regression a genuine customer-lifetime-value model.
**More data.** Usage, complaints, network quality and competitor offers would help explain churn among long-tenure customers.
**More methods.** Larger settings grids, cross-validation, regularised regression and boosting methods can be tried once the basic comparison is understood.
**Business evaluation.** Attach costs and benefits to retention offers and choose the threshold that maximises profit, ideally using a randomised experiment.
**Time-based validation.** With dated data, train on the past and test on the future.
**Deployment.** Wrap the saved models in a simple application (src/predict.py is a starting point) and monitor their accuracy over time.
**Local data.** Repeat the study on an authentic telecom data set from an open-data portal.
